laws.subtitle: Brazil reverses deforestation trend under new environmental policy
laws.fullDescription: Under President Lula, Brazil significantly reduced Amazon deforestation, reversing the increases under Bolsonaro. Annual deforestation fell by over 50% in 2023 compared to the previous year. Brazil hosts COP30 in Belém in 2025, positioning itself as a climate leader. However, pressures from agribusiness, mining, and infrastructure remain. Brazil's agricultural success (world's largest soybean and beef exporter) creates ongoing tension with forest protection. The government promotes sustainable development models for the Amazon.
laws.penalty: Illegal deforestation carries criminal penalties and property confiscation under the Forest Code
exceptions: Legal deforestation within permitted limits continues for agriculture and development
Small farmers under 4 fiscal modules exempt from some restoration requirements

laws.title: Agribusiness Superpower and Deforestation Dilemma
laws.subtitle: Brazil feeds the world while debating its forest
laws.fullDescription: Brazil is the world's largest exporter of soybeans, beef, chicken, sugar, coffee, and orange juice — an agricultural superpower that feeds billions. The agribusiness sector (agronegócio) represents 25% of GDP and has enormous political power. The tension between expanding agricultural production (often into frontier lands) and deforestation is Brazil's central environmental dilemma. The EU's deforestation regulation requiring supply chain proof of no deforestation threatens Brazilian agricultural exports.
laws.penalty: EU Deforestation Regulation requires importers to verify Brazilian products come from deforestation-free land
exceptions: Products certified under recognized sustainability schemes qualify for simplified compliance
Small-scale producers have different requirements than large commercial operations

laws.title: Football Economy and CBF Corruption Reforms
laws.subtitle: Brazil's football confederation battles corruption while producing global stars
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's football (soccer) culture is globally dominant — five World Cup titles, legendary players (Pelé, Ronaldo, Neymar, Vinicius Jr.). The Confederação Brasileira de Futebol (CBF) has faced massive corruption scandals, with officials imprisoned in the FIFA corruption case. Brazil reforms football governance while the sport generates massive economic activity. Brazilian players command the world's highest transfer fees. Brazil co-hosts the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and competed for 2030 hosting.
laws.penalty: CBF must comply with transparency and integrity standards as FIFA governance requirements
exceptions: Youth academies have different regulatory requirements from professional clubs
Amateur football federations operate under simplified compliance requirements

quiz.q: How many FIFA World Cups has Brazil won?
quiz.explanation: Brazil has won five FIFA World Cups (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, 2002) — more than any other nation — cementing its status as the world's most successful footballing country and the sport's cultural heartland.

laws.title: Amazon Deforestation Reversal and COP30 Presidency
laws.subtitle: Brazil's environmental policy turnaround under Lula
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lula government (returned to power in January 2023) has reversed the deforestation surge of the Bolsonaro years, with Amazon deforestation rates dropping dramatically. The government re-established IBAMA's enforcement capacity, implemented satellite monitoring, and pursued operations against illegal miners (garimpeiros) — including expelling thousands from Yanomami Indigenous territory where illegal gold mining had caused a humanitarian crisis. Brazil is hosting COP30 in Belém, in the Amazon region, in November 2025 — a symbolic choice emphasizing the link between climate action and Amazon protection. Brazil is simultaneously one of the world's largest agricultural producers (soybeans, beef, sugar, coffee) and holds the world's largest tropical forest. The tension between agricultural development interests and environmental protection is central to Brazilian politics. Brazil also has significant offshore oil reserves being developed by Petrobras, creating a paradox for its climate leadership aspirations.
laws.penalty: Environmental crimes including illegal deforestation carry criminal penalties and fines; Amazon protection zones have enforcement mechanisms
exceptions: Legal deforestation limits exist for different biomes and land categories

quiz.q: Where is Brazil hosting COP30 in 2025, and why is the location symbolic?
options: Rio de Janeiro, as Brazil's most famous city
Belém, in the Amazon region, linking climate action to forest protection
São Paulo, as Brazil's economic center
quiz.explanation: Brazil is hosting COP30 in Belém, located in the Amazon region, a symbolically powerful choice emphasizing the connection between global climate action and protection of the world's largest tropical forest.

laws.title: Agribusiness Powerhouse and Deforestation Trade-offs
laws.subtitle: Brazil feeding the world while deforesting its heritage
laws.fullDescription: Brazil is one of the world's most critical agricultural nations — the largest exporter of soybeans, beef, chicken, orange juice, sugar, and coffee, and a major supplier of corn. Brazilian agribusiness has achieved remarkable productivity gains through science-based agriculture adapted for tropical soils. However, the expansion of agriculture has been a primary driver of deforestation in the Amazon, Cerrado (savanna), and Pantanal — ecosystems of global climate significance. The Cerrado, though receiving less attention than the Amazon, has been particularly devastated, with more than half converted to agriculture. Brazilian agricultural and environmental law creates tension between property rights, environmental requirements (the Forest Code mandating legal reserves), and commercial interests. International buyers — particularly European — have pressed for deforestation-free supply chains, and the EU Deforestation Regulation requires proof of deforestation-free production.
laws.penalty: Environmental violations including illegal deforestation carry criminal penalties and fines under Brazilian law; embargoed lands cannot sell products legally
exceptions: The Forest Code has different requirements for different biomes and farm sizes

quiz.q: What does the EU Deforestation Regulation require of Brazilian exporters?
options: A carbon tax on all agricultural exports
Proof that products are deforestation-free before entering EU markets
Certification from the Brazilian government of sustainable practices
quiz.explanation: The EU Deforestation Regulation requires that agricultural commodities sold in the EU — including soy, beef, coffee, and palm oil — come with proof that they are not linked to deforestation, creating significant compliance requirements for Brazilian exporters.

laws.title: Amazon Fund Reactivation
laws.subtitle: Deforestation reversal via international green finance
laws.fullDescription: Brazil reactivated its Amazon Fund in 2023 after years of suspension, receiving billions from Norway, Germany and the EU. The fund finances deforestation monitoring, indigenous land protection and sustainable agriculture. Deforestation dropped significantly in Lula's first year but remains well above zero. Critics note enforcement gaps and illegal gold mining persist in protected zones.
laws.penalty: Fund disbursements tied to deforestation metrics; projects receiving funds must meet strict sustainability criteria
exceptions: Small-scale subsistence farming exempt
Legal selective logging with environmental permits allowed

quiz.q: Which countries are the biggest donors to Brazil's Amazon Fund?
quiz.explanation: Norway and Germany are the primary donors to the Amazon Fund, which finances deforestation prevention efforts in the Brazilian Amazon.

laws.title: Lula Fiscal Responsibility vs Spending Pressure
laws.subtitle: Real weakens as markets doubt Brazil's fiscal framework
laws.fullDescription: President Lula's third term faced market skepticism about Brazil's fiscal trajectory. The government repeatedly sent mixed signals—announcing spending cuts while simultaneously pushing new social programs. The Brazilian real weakened significantly against the dollar. The central bank, under its independent framework, raised interest rates aggressively to contain inflation. Lula publicly blamed high interest rates for stalling growth, creating tension with the independent monetary authority that became a defining feature of his economic governance.
laws.penalty: Brazil's fiscal framework sets spending caps; violations trigger automatic stabilizers and loss of fiscal anchor credibility
exceptions: Constitutionally mandated spending on health and education exempt from some caps
Extraordinary disaster spending allowed outside normal limits

quiz.q: What did President Lula blame for stalling Brazil's economic growth?
options: High interest rates set by the independent central bank
quiz.explanation: Lula publicly blamed Brazil's high interest rates, set by the independent central bank under its inflation-targeting mandate, for stalling economic growth—creating public tension with monetary authorities.

laws.title: Pix Instant Payment Revolution
laws.subtitle: Brazil's central bank payment system transforms financial access
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Pix instant payment system, launched by the central bank in 2020, became one of the world's most successful financial technology deployments. Within three years, over 150 million Brazilians were using Pix for instant transfers, bill payments and merchant transactions at any hour. The system operates 24/7, charges minimal fees and is interoperable across all banks. Pix dramatically expanded financial inclusion and disrupted traditional card networks. Brazil's central bank-run open finance ecosystem has become a global model for financial infrastructure.
laws.penalty: Banks required to participate in Pix; blocking or delaying Pix transactions subject to central bank sanctions
exceptions: Small fintechs have phased participation requirements
System automatically processes transactions with fraud monitoring

quiz.q: How many Brazilians were using Pix within three years of its 2020 launch?
quiz.explanation: Over 150 million Brazilians were using Pix within three years of its 2020 launch, making it one of the world's most successful instant payment system rollouts and a global model for central bank-run payment infrastructure.

laws.title: Agribusiness Giant and Cerrado Expansion
laws.subtitle: Brazil dominates global soy, beef and corn markets
laws.fullDescription: Brazil has become the world's largest exporter of soybeans, beef, chicken and a major corn exporter, driven by expansion into the Cerrado savanna. The Cerrado—Brazil's vast interior savanna—has been transformed into agricultural land at enormous scale. Brazilian agribusiness represents about 25% of GDP. The expansion has converted significant native Cerrado vegetation, which stores enormous carbon despite being less famous than the Amazon. Brazilian agribusiness lobbies are politically powerful and resist environmental regulations.
laws.penalty: Deforestation in Cerrado not as restricted as Amazon; rural environmental registry tracks land use on agricultural properties
exceptions: Legal Reserve requirements mandate preservation of some native vegetation on farm properties
Conservation easements available for landowners preserving native Cerrado

quiz.q: What is the Cerrado?
options: Brazil's vast interior savanna being converted to agriculture
Brazil's mountain rainforest in the south
quiz.explanation: The Cerrado is Brazil's vast interior savanna that has been transformed into agricultural land at enormous scale, making Brazil the world's top exporter of soybeans and beef—while storing significant carbon despite being less famous than the Amazon.

laws.title: Amazon Deforestation Law
laws.subtitle: Protecting the Lungs of the Planet
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Forest Code (Lei 12.651/2012) requires landowners in the Amazon to preserve 80% of their property as native forest, known as the Legal Reserve. Deforestation reached crisis levels under President Bolsonaro (2019-2022) but dropped sharply after President Lula took office in 2023, pledging zero illegal deforestation by 2030. The Environmental Rural Registry (CAR) maps all rural properties, enabling satellite monitoring. Brazil's Amazon Fund, supported by Norway and Germany, finances conservation.
laws.penalty: Fines of R$5,000 to R$50 million per hectare of illegal deforestation; property embargoes; criminal charges
exceptions: Traditional communities and indigenous territories
Small family farms under different reserve requirements
Legal selective logging with permits

laws.title: Brazil's Unified Health System (SUS)
laws.subtitle: Universal Healthcare as Constitutional Right
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Unified Health System (SUS — Sistema Único de Saúde), established by the 1988 Constitution, provides universal free healthcare to all Brazilian citizens. SUS is one of the world's largest public health systems, serving 150+ million people. Brazil has achieved remarkable public health successes through SUS: HIV/AIDS treatment program (generic antiretrovirals), vaccination campaigns, and control of tropical diseases. Pharmaceutical access is guaranteed by law, and Brazil has broken patents on essential medicines. However, SUS faces chronic underfunding, regional inequality, and long wait times for specialized care.
laws.penalty: Municipalities must spend 15% and states 12% of tax revenue on health; constitutional violation if not met
exceptions: Private healthcare plans operate in parallel
Military personnel under separate system

laws.title: Brazil Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT)
laws.subtitle: Vargas's Labor Legacy
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), created by President Getúlio Vargas in 1943, is one of Latin America's most comprehensive labor codes — governing employment contracts, working hours, wages, vacation, termination, and social security. Brazil's 2017 Labor Reform (under President Temer) weakened some CLT protections, allowing collective bargaining to override statutory minimums and expanding part-time and intermittent work. President Lula's return to power (2023) signaled possible restoration of some protections. Brazil's Fundo de Garantia do Tempo de Serviço (FGTS) requires employers to deposit 8% of monthly wages into a worker's account, available upon termination.
laws.penalty: CLT violations: labor court awards; FGTS non-deposit: fines and back-deposit with interest; unfair dismissal: severance
exceptions: Domestic workers under simplified regime
Rural workers have adapted provisions

laws.title: Brazil PROUNI and University Quotas
laws.subtitle: Black and Indigenous Affirmative Action
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's ProUni program provides full or partial scholarships to low-income students for private university enrollment, linked to tax exemptions for participating universities. Brazil's Law 12.711/2012 mandated racial quotas in federal universities — reserving 50% of federal university places for public school graduates, with sub-quotas for Black, mixed-race (pardo), and Indigenous students proportional to their state demographic share. The Supreme Court upheld racial quotas in 2023. Brazil's FIES (student financing) program provides income-contingent loans. Brazil also has universal free public education from kindergarten through public university.
laws.penalty: Universities receiving ProUni tax benefits must maintain quota commitments; FIES loan misuse: criminal liability
exceptions: Private universities can opt out of ProUni
Quota formulas adjusted by state demographics

laws.title: Migration Law (Lei de Migração)
laws.subtitle: Brazil's rights-based immigration framework
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Migration Law (Law 13,445/2017) replaced a military-era law dating from 1980, adopting a rights-based approach to immigration. The law guarantees immigrants equal civil rights to Brazilians (bank accounts, access to public services, education, healthcare), eliminates the concept of the 'national security' deportation, creates humanitarian visa categories, and establishes regularization pathways. Brazil has been particularly notable for providing humanitarian visas to Haitians (after 2010 earthquake) and Venezuelans fleeing economic collapse — over 400,000 Venezuelan immigrants regularized.
laws.penalty: Deportation requires administrative due process; employers exploiting immigrant workers face labor law penalties; human trafficking of migrants is a serious crime with 4-8 year sentences
exceptions: MERCOSUR citizens have simplified residency rights under the Residence Agreement
Humanitarian visa holders (Haitian, Venezuelan) receive expedited regularization

quiz.q: Brazil's 2017 Migration Law replaced a law from which era that treated immigration primarily as a security issue?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's 2017 Migration Law replaced the Statute of Foreigners from 1980, enacted during the military dictatorship, which framed immigration primarily as a national security matter. The new law adopted a human rights framework instead.

laws.title: Drug Law and Possession Dilemma
laws.subtitle: Brazil's drug law that fails to distinguish user from trafficker
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Drug Law (11,343/2006) removed criminal penalties for drug possession for personal use (no jail time) but failed to define what quantity distinguishes personal use from trafficking — leaving this determination to judges. This ambiguity has led to racial disparity: Black Brazilians are far more likely to be classified as traffickers than white Brazilians with similar amounts. Trafficking carries 5-15 years imprisonment. Brazil has massive drug trafficking organizations (CV, PCC) that control territories in favelas. Brazil has the world's third-largest cocaine consumer market.
laws.penalty: Personal drug use: not criminalized (education/treatment mandated); drug trafficking: 5-15 years (can increase 1/6 to 2/3 based on quantity, type, gang involvement); organized drug trafficking: penalties doubled; drug trafficking causing death: up to life in some interpretations
exceptions: Personal use possession is decriminalized but not defined by quantity
First-time offenders may receive treatment instead of prosecution
Pregnant women trafficking small amounts may receive house arrest

quiz.q: Brazil's 2006 Drug Law left which critical question undefined, leading to racial disparities in prosecution?
options: What quantity distinguishes personal use from drug trafficking
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Drug Law decriminalized personal use but failed to set quantity thresholds distinguishing personal use from trafficking — leaving this to judicial discretion. Studies show Black Brazilians are far more likely to be classified as traffickers than white Brazilians found with similar quantities.

laws.title: STF Criminalization of Homophobia and Trans Rights
laws.subtitle: Brazil's judicial LGBTQ+ protections amid violence
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Supreme Court (STF) ruled in 2019 that homophobia and transphobia constitute crimes under the existing racism law, since Congress had failed to legislate. Brazil legalized same-sex civil unions (2011, by Supreme Court) and same-sex marriage (2013, by National Justice Council). Brazil has the world's highest rate of LGBTQ+ murders. Under Bolsonaro (2019-2022), anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric increased. Under Lula (2022+), protections were restored. Brazil's Trans community has disproportionate rates of violence — Brazil records 160+ trans murders annually, 40%+ of global total.
laws.penalty: Homophobia/transphobia crimes: same penalties as racism (imprisonment 1-3 years, increased if committed by authority or in public); LGBTQ+ hate murder: homicide with aggravated penalties; discrimination in employment/services: civil and criminal liability
exceptions: Religious freedom arguments for discriminatory church speech have some protection
Marriage registered through federal courts has greater enforceability than some state implementations
laws.sourceLabel: Brazil STF ADO 26 Decision (2019) – Criminalization of Homophobia

quiz.q: Brazil criminalized homophobia and transphobia in 2019 through a ruling by which institution, after Congress failed to act?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF) ruled in June 2019 that homophobia and transphobia constitute crimes under the existing anti-racism law, applying the crime of 'racism' to LGBTQ+ discrimination. This was a judicial remedy after Congress had failed to pass LGBTQ+ non-discrimination legislation for over 20 years.

laws.title: Press Freedom Under Threat — Journalist Violence and Political Attacks
laws.subtitle: Brazil's constitution protects press freedom but journalists face violence, especially in rural areas
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's constitution guarantees freedom of the press (Article 220) and prohibits censorship. However, Brazil consistently ranks among the world's most dangerous countries for journalists, particularly those covering environmental issues, land rights, and organized crime in rural areas. During Bolsonaro's presidency (2019-2022), attacks on the press intensified. The Lula administration restored some normalcy. The Lei de Imprensa (Press Law) was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2009. Digital platforms and disinformation have created new challenges. The journalist Dom Phillips was murdered in the Amazon in 2022.
laws.penalty: No formal censorship law; criminal defamation exists but press has broad constitutional protection; journalist murders are serious ongoing issue
exceptions: Criminal defamation (calúnia, injúria, difamação) can be used against journalists

quiz.q: What happened to journalist Dom Phillips in Brazil in 2022, highlighting press freedom dangers?
options: He was murdered in the Amazon
His outlet was closed by court order
quiz.explanation: British journalist Dom Phillips was murdered in the Amazon in June 2022 while reporting on threats to Indigenous communities and environmental defenders — his murder highlighted the extreme dangers faced by journalists covering rural Brazil.

laws.title: LGPD — Brazil's Comprehensive Data Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Brazil's General Data Protection Law applies to all digital platforms including social media
laws.fullDescription: Brazil enacted the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD) in 2018, effective 2020, modeled on the EU's GDPR. The LGPD gives Brazilians rights to access, correct, delete, and port their data. The National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) enforces the law. Brazil also has the Marco Civil da Internet (2014), a comprehensive internet civil rights framework guaranteeing net neutrality, privacy, and freedom of expression online. Brazil has been active in regulating social media: a 2023 Supreme Court ruling required platforms to remove content deemed undemocratic, and the ANPD has fined major companies.
laws.penalty: LGPD: fines up to 2% of Brazil revenue (max R$50 million) per incident; ANPD enforcement authority
exceptions: National security and law enforcement have exemptions

quiz.q: What is Brazil's Marco Civil da Internet and why is it significant?
options: A law restricting social media use
A comprehensive internet civil rights framework guaranteeing net neutrality and online rights
A law requiring internet service provider registration
A social media content moderation mandate
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Marco Civil da Internet (2014) is a landmark comprehensive internet rights framework that guarantees net neutrality, privacy protections, freedom of expression online, and limits intermediary liability — often called the 'Internet Constitution' and influential globally as a model.

laws.title: PIX Instant Payment System and Fintech Revolution
laws.subtitle: Brazil's PIX is the world's most successful instant payment system with 150+ million users
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Central Bank launched PIX in November 2020 — an instant payment system that within two years became one of the world's most successful digital payment platforms with over 150 million users (in a country of 215 million). PIX allows instant free transfers 24/7 between individuals, businesses, and government. Brazil's Banking Law (4,595/1964) and financial regulations are overseen by the Banco Central. Brazil also created the Open Banking/Open Finance framework (2020-2023) requiring banks to share customer data with authorized fintechs. Brazil's fintech sector is one of Latin America's most vibrant.
laws.penalty: Banco Central regulatory enforcement; PIX system violations subject to penalties; Open Finance non-compliance fined
exceptions: Smaller financial institutions have extended timelines for Open Finance compliance

quiz.q: What achievement distinguishes Brazil's PIX payment system globally?
options: It was the first digital currency
It became one of the world's most successful instant payment systems with 150+ million users within two years
It eliminated all cash usage in Brazil
It was the first cross-border payment system
quiz.explanation: Brazil's PIX, launched in November 2020, became one of the world's most successful instant payment systems, reaching over 150 million users in a country of 215 million within two years — enabling free, 24/7 instant transfers and dramatically accelerating Brazil's financial inclusion.

laws.title: ANVISA Food Safety Regulation & RDC Food Standards
laws.subtitle: Brazil's health regulator ANVISA sets comprehensive food safety and labeling standards
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's National Health Surveillance Agency (ANVISA) is responsible for food safety regulation for all food products marketed in Brazil. ANVISA issues Resoluções da Diretoria Colegiada (RDCs) — regulatory decisions covering food composition, labeling, additives, contaminants, and hygiene. Brazil implemented mandatory front-of-packaging warning labels (black octagonal warning signs) in 2022 for foods high in sugar, saturated fat, and sodium — among the most visible food labeling systems in the world. The Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Food Supply (MAPA) oversees food of animal origin. Brazil's food safety system is critical given it's the world's largest exporter of chicken, beef, sugar, and soybeans.
laws.penalty: ANVISA violations: fines from BRL 2,000 to BRL 1.5 million per infraction; selling adulterated food: criminal charges under the Consumers Defense Code; labeling violations: product recalls
exceptions: Artisanal foods (queijo de coalho, artisanal cachaça) have modified production standards
Indigenous communities' traditional food production has cultural exceptions
Small rural producers for local consumption have simplified rules

quiz.q: What distinctive front-of-package warning system did Brazil implement in 2022 for processed foods?
options: Red traffic light system for fats/sugar/salt
Black octagonal warning signs for foods high in sugar, saturated fat, or sodium
QR codes linking to full nutritional analysis
quiz.explanation: Brazil's ANVISA implemented mandatory black octagonal warning signs (similar to stop signs) on the front of packaged foods that are high in added sugars, saturated fats, or sodium — one of the world's most prominent and recognizable front-of-pack warning label systems.

laws.title: Brazil Federal Animal Cruelty Law and Lei Arouca
laws.subtitle: Brazil's Constitution and Lei Arouca protect animal welfare
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Federal Law 9.605/1998 (Environmental Crimes Law) criminalizes animal abuse — it was a landmark because animal cruelty became a criminal offense at the federal level for the first time. Lei Arouca (Federal Law 11.794/2008) regulates scientific animal use, requiring ethics committees. The 1988 Federal Constitution Article 225 §1 VII explicitly prohibits practices that cause animal cruelty. Brazil also has state-level animal welfare laws in São Paulo and other major states banning exotic animals in circuses. Brazil banned animal experimentation for cosmetics (Lei 15.316/2020). The country, however, still has significant enforcement gaps especially in rural areas.
laws.penalty: Federal law: 3 months to 1 year imprisonment for cruelty (increased to 2–5 years by Lei 14.064/2020 for dogs and cats); fines vary by state
exceptions: Livestock slaughter under federal oversight
Licensed hunting in specific regions
Scientific research under Lei Arouca ethics committees

quiz.q: What change did Brazil's Lei 14.064/2020 make to animal cruelty penalties?
options: It increased penalties for cruelty to dogs and cats to 2–5 years imprisonment
It created a national animal registry
It banned all exotic pet ownership
quiz.explanation: Lei 14.064/2020 significantly increased criminal penalties for animal cruelty specifically against dogs and cats — raising the sentence from 3 months–1 year to 2–5 years imprisonment, following public outcry over high-profile animal abuse cases.

laws.title: Brazil Family Law — Civil Code 2002 and Stable Union
laws.subtitle: Brazil recognizes stable unions with near-equal rights to marriage
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's family law is governed by the Civil Code 2002 (Código Civil) and constitutional provisions. Brazil has two main recognized family relationships: marriage and estável (stable union) — cohabitation relationships. Brazil's Supreme Court (STF) ruled in 2011 that same-sex stable unions have the same rights as opposite-sex unions. Brazil allows extrajudicial divorce — couples without children or disputes can divorce directly at a notary (cartório) without court involvement, a significant efficiency improvement. Property regimes: Community of acquired property (partial community) is the default — assets acquired during the marriage are shared. Brazil also has strong provisions for legal acknowledgment of children born outside marriage.
laws.penalty: Family court civil enforcement; child support (alimentos) enforced with potential civil imprisonment for 1–3 months for willful non-payment; contempt for order violations
exceptions: Pre-marital property (bens particulares)
Gifts and inheritances
Couples can choose different property regimes by prenuptial agreement

quiz.q: What efficient divorce option does Brazil offer to couples without children or disputes?
options: Extrajudicial divorce at a notary (cartório) — no court required
quiz.explanation: Brazil allows extrajudicial divorce — couples with no children under 18 and no disputes can divorce directly at a notary office (cartório) without going to court. This was introduced to reduce court backlogs and is a significant efficiency innovation that multiple other countries have adopted.

laws.title: Brazil Estatuto da Cidade & Urban Property Rights
laws.subtitle: Social function of property and urban land reform
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Estatuto da Cidade (City Statute, Law 10.257/2001) establishes that urban property must fulfill a 'social function' (funcao social da propriedade), enshrined in the 1988 Constitution (Art. 5, XXII-XXIII). Municipalities can compel underused urban land to be developed through progressive IPTU taxation (IPTU progressivo), and ultimately expropriate it for social housing at below-market rates. The Minha Casa Minha Vida program has built over 5 million subsidized homes. Squatter settlements (favelas) have complex informal property rights addressed by the Lei de Regularizacao Fundiaria (Law 13.465/2017).
laws.penalty: Progressive IPTU tax up to 15% for non-compliant property; expropriation for social interest at assessed value
exceptions: Social function doctrine limits purely speculative land holding
Adverse possession (usucapiao) after 5 years for residential use
laws.source: Lei 10.257/2001; Constituicao Federal Art. 5 XXII-XXIII; Lei 13.465/2017

quiz.q: What is the core principle underlying Brazil's City Statute regarding urban property?
options: Property must fulfill a social function
All land belongs to the state
quiz.explanation: The City Statute (Estatuto da Cidade) implements the constitutional principle that urban property must fulfill a 'social function' (funcao social), allowing municipalities to act against underused or idle land.

laws.title: Brazil Codigo de Defesa do Consumidor (CDC)
laws.subtitle: Latin America's pioneering consumer protection code
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Codigo de Defesa do Consumidor (CDC, Law 8.078/1990) is one of the world's most comprehensive consumer protection codes and a model for Latin America. It establishes strict liability for product defects, reversal of the burden of proof in consumer disputes, a 7-day cooling-off period for off-premises purchases, and broad prohibitions on abusive contract terms. PROCON consumer protection agencies operate in each state to mediate disputes. The CDC applies to digital services and e-commerce via the Decreto 7962/2013. Brazil's Superior Tribunal de Justica (STJ) regularly expands consumer rights through case law. Class actions under the CDC are powerful enforcement tools.
laws.penalty: Product liability: strict liability for manufacturers; abusive clauses: void; PROCON fine up to BRL 10 million
exceptions: 7-day cooling-off period for distance and off-premises purchases
Burden of proof reversal in favor of consumers in disputes

quiz.q: What burden of proof rule does Brazil's CDC (Consumer Defense Code) establish in consumer disputes?
options: Burden of proof is reversed in favor of the consumer
Government proves harm on behalf of consumer
quiz.explanation: Brazil's CDC (Article 6, VIII) allows courts to reverse the burden of proof in consumer disputes when the consumer's claim is plausible and they are technically at a disadvantage — one of the most powerful procedural protections in consumer law worldwide.

laws.title: Lei Maria da Penha — Domestic Violence Law
laws.subtitle: Law 11.340/2006 — landmark domestic violence protection
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lei Maria da Penha (Law 11.340/2006) is considered one of the world's strongest domestic violence laws, named after Maria da Penha Maia Fernandes who campaigned after surviving an assassination attempt by her husband. The law creates special courts for domestic violence, allows protective measures within 48 hours, increases penalties for domestic violence, and prohibits perpetrators from contacting victims. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights case against Brazil helped spark the legislation.
laws.penalty: Domestic violence: 3 months to 3 years imprisonment. Femicide (Lei do Feminicídio, 2015): 12-30 years.
exceptions: Lesbian couples also protected under expanded interpretations
Protective orders available regardless of marital status
Emergency measures available 24/7 via DEAM (women's police stations)

quiz.q: Who is Brazil's Lei Maria da Penha named after?
options: A congresswoman who drafted the law
A woman who survived a domestic violence assassination attempt
quiz.explanation: The law is named after Maria da Penha Maia Fernandes, who survived two assassination attempts by her husband and campaigned for stronger domestic violence protections. An Inter-American Commission on Human Rights ruling against Brazil for failure to prosecute her case helped lead to the landmark 2006 legislation.

laws.title: Amazon Forest Code — Lei da Mata Atlântica
laws.subtitle: Forest Code (Law 12.651/2012) — 80% Amazon protection
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Forest Code (Lei 12.651/2012) requires rural landowners in the Amazon biome to maintain 80% of their land as native vegetation (Legal Reserve). Atlantic Forest landowners must maintain 20%. The law also protects permanent preservation areas (APPs) along rivers and on hillsides. A controversial 2012 reform granted amnesty for pre-2008 deforestation violations. IBAMA enforces the code with fines and embargos on illegally deforested land.
laws.penalty: Illegal deforestation: fines up to R$1,500/hectare, property embargo, criminal prosecution (1-3 years + fines).
exceptions: Small rural producers (up to 4 fiscal modules) have simplified APP restoration requirements
Indigenous lands managed under separate framework
Consolidated areas (pre-2008 deforestation) have reduced restoration requirements

quiz.q: What percentage of Amazon biome land must rural landowners maintain as native vegetation under Brazil's Forest Code?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Forest Code requires that rural landowners in the Amazon biome maintain 80% of their land as native vegetation (Reserva Legal). In the Atlantic Forest, the requirement is 20%. This legal reserve must be maintained and cannot be cleared without authorization.

laws.title: Bolsa Família — Conditional Cash Transfer
laws.subtitle: Brazil's flagship poverty reduction program
laws.fullDescription: Bolsa Família, created in 2003 under President Lula and later transformed into Auxílio Brasil (2021) and back to Bolsa Família (2023), is Brazil's flagship conditional cash transfer program. It provides monthly payments to low-income families conditional on keeping children in school and meeting vaccination requirements. At peak, it covered over 14 million families. Studies show it significantly reduced extreme poverty and malnutrition. The program is widely credited as a global model for social protection.
laws.penalty: Benefit fraud: repayment of overpayments, disqualification, criminal prosecution for fraud.
exceptions: Refugee families may qualify regardless of documentation status
Quilombola communities have priority enrollment
Emergency benefits during COVID-19 expanded coverage significantly
laws.sourceLabel: Ministério do Desenvolvimento Social — Bolsa Família

quiz.q: What conditions must Bolsa Família recipient families meet to continue receiving benefits?
options: Keeping children in school and meeting vaccination requirements
quiz.explanation: Bolsa Família is a conditional cash transfer — recipients must keep children enrolled in school (minimum 85% attendance) and meet vaccination and prenatal care requirements. These conditions link the cash transfer to human capital development in health and education.

laws.title: Lei Anticorrupção — Brazil's Anti-Corruption Law
laws.subtitle: Law 12.846/2013 — corporate liability for corruption
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lei Anticorrupção (Law 12.846/2013) establishes objective (strict) liability for legal entities for corrupt acts against national and foreign governments. Companies can be fined up to 20% of gross revenue. The law was passed following the Mensalão scandal and preceded the Lava Jato (Car Wash) investigation that uncovered massive corruption at Petrobras. Brazil's CGU (federal comptroller) enforces the law. Leniency agreements allow companies to reduce penalties in exchange for cooperation.
laws.penalty: Corporate fines: 0.1%-20% of gross revenue. Publication of condemnation. Dissolution of legal entity for severe cases.
exceptions: Leniency agreements reduce fines for cooperating companies
Small companies (microempresas) have reduced fine caps
Individual employees prosecuted under separate criminal code

quiz.q: What is the maximum fine for companies convicted under Brazil's Lei Anticorrupção?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Lei Anticorrupção allows fines of up to 20% of gross annual revenue for the year preceding the investigation, applied to companies found guilty of corrupt acts against national or foreign governments. The law establishes strict (objective) liability — intent does not need to be proven.

laws.title: Estatuto do Desarmamento — Disarmament Statute
laws.subtitle: Law 10.826/2003 — strict civilian gun controls
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Estatuto do Desarmamento (Law 10.826/2003) established strict firearm controls: civilians must be 25+, have clean record, demonstrate need (for carry permit), and pass psychological and technical testing. Carry permits are rarely granted. A 2019 Bolsonaro decree loosened some restrictions for rural workers and collectors, but the Supreme Court blocked the broadest changes. Brazil remains extremely violent despite controls — over 40,000 firearm deaths annually — because illegal guns are ubiquitous.
laws.penalty: Illegal possession: 2-4 years. Illegal carry: 3-5 years. Trafficking: 4-8 years.
exceptions: Law enforcement and security professionals have broader access
Rural landowners (propriedade rural) have modified requirements
Registered collectors (CAC) may possess with significant paperwork

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to legally possess a firearm in Brazil under the Estatuto do Desarmamento?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Estatuto do Desarmamento requires a minimum age of 25 to possess a firearm legally. This is higher than most countries. Additionally, applicants must have a clean criminal record, demonstrate psychological fitness, and pass technical testing. Carry permits require proving genuine need, which is rarely granted.

laws.title: Cotas Raciais — Racial Quota System
laws.subtitle: Law 12.711/2012 — university quotas for Black, indigenous students
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's quota law (Lei das Cotas, 12.711/2012) reserves 50% of federal university places for public school graduates, with sub-quotas for Black (preto/pardo), indigenous, and disabled students proportional to their state population. The law was upheld by Brazil's Supreme Court in 2012. Brazil's racial quota system is one of the most comprehensive in the world, addressing the legacy of slavery (abolished 1888) and deep socioeconomic inequality. Some states have extended quotas to public service jobs.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for quota violations — enforcement through university admission systems. Fraud in racial self-declaration investigated by committees.
exceptions: Private universities not covered by federal law
Some states and municipalities have broader quota laws
Quota candidates may choose to compete in general pool if more competitive

quiz.q: What percentage of federal university places does Brazil's quota law reserve for public school graduates?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Lei das Cotas reserves 50% of federal university places for students who completed secondary education entirely in public schools. Within that 50%, sub-quotas allocate spots for self-declared Black, mixed-race (pardo), indigenous, and disabled students proportional to the state's population.

laws.title: Petrobras Law — Pre-Salt Oil Sharing
laws.subtitle: Law 12.351/2010 — production sharing for pre-salt oil
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's pre-salt oil discoveries (2006-2007) revealed one of the world's largest oil reserves beneath a deep salt layer off the coast. Law 12.351/2010 established a production sharing regime for pre-salt areas, with Petrobras as mandatory operator with minimum 30% stake. The federal government receives the majority of oil revenue through profit oil and royalties. Revenue is constitutionally earmarked for education and healthcare. The pre-salt fields now account for over 70% of Brazil's oil production.
laws.penalty: Petrobras contract violations: civil penalties, production suspension. License revocation for non-compliance.
exceptions: Small pre-salt discoveries may be licensed under concession model
Petrobras minimum stake requirement reduced in 2019 for some blocks
Foreign operators can form consortia with Petrobras as operator

quiz.q: What is Petrobras's mandatory minimum stake in pre-salt oil production under Brazilian law?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's pre-salt law requires Petrobras to hold a minimum 30% stake in all pre-salt production sharing contracts, serving as mandatory operator. This requirement was designed to ensure the state oil company benefits from Brazil's massive pre-salt discoveries, which were announced in 2006-2007.

laws.title: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados — LGPD
laws.subtitle: Law 13.709/2018 — Brazil's GDPR equivalent
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD, Law 13.709/2018) regulates the processing of personal data, modeled on Europe's GDPR. It creates rights for data subjects (access, correction, deletion, portability), requires lawful basis for processing, and mandates data protection officers for certain organizations. The ANPD (National Data Protection Authority) enforces the law. Fines can reach 2% of Brazilian revenues up to R$50 million per violation. LGPD applies to any processing involving data of persons in Brazil.
laws.penalty: Administrative fines up to 2% of Brazil revenue (max R$50 million per violation). Public disclosure of violation. Suspension of processing.
exceptions: Journalistic and academic research has modified requirements
National security and public safety processing exempt from some provisions
Individual non-commercial data processing generally exempt

quiz.q: What is the maximum administrative fine under Brazil's LGPD?
options: 2% of revenue up to R$50 million
quiz.explanation: Brazil's LGPD allows administrative fines of up to 2% of Brazilian revenues in the year prior to investigation, capped at R$50 million per violation. The ANPD (National Data Protection Authority) has enforcement powers similar to Europe's GDPR regulators.

laws.title: Código de Trânsito Brasileiro — Blood Alcohol Zero
laws.subtitle: CTB — zero tolerance: 0.05mg/L blood alcohol limit
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Traffic Code (CTB) establishes near-zero tolerance for drunk driving: the administrative limit is 0.05mg/L blood alcohol (reduced from 0.06g/L by the 'Dry Law'/Lei Seca in 2012). Criminal prosecution begins at 0.3mg/L. Brazil's traffic violence is among the world's worst — about 33,000 deaths annually. Operation Balada Segura conducts roadside breathalyzer checkpoints. Refusing a breathalyzer is treated as if the limit was exceeded.
laws.penalty: 0.05-0.30mg/L: R$2,934 fine, 12-month license suspension, vehicle seizure. Above 0.30mg/L: criminal — 6 months to 3 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Drivers on prescribed medications affecting BAC may contest with medical documentation
Commercial drivers have stricter limits
Motorcycle riders subject to same limits

quiz.q: What is Brazil's administrative blood alcohol limit for driving under the Lei Seca?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Lei Seca (Dry Law) sets a near-zero administrative blood alcohol limit of 0.05mg/L. Criminal prosecution begins at 0.3mg/L. Refusing a breathalyzer test is treated as if the driver exceeded the limit.

laws.title: SUS — Sistema Único de Saúde
laws.subtitle: Brazil's universal public health system
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's SUS (Sistema Único de Saúde), created by the 1988 Constitution, provides universal healthcare to all Brazilian residents free of charge, regardless of income or immigration status. SUS serves approximately 75% of Brazilians (those without private insurance). It is the world's largest public health system by population served. The system covers everything from primary care to organ transplants. Chronic underfunding relative to population needs remains a major challenge. Constitutional Amendment 29 (2000) established minimum health spending floors.
laws.penalty: No penalties for patients. Providers who defraud SUS face criminal prosecution, fines, and exclusion from the system.
exceptions: Private complementary health plans operate alongside SUS
Foreign tourists may access emergency SUS care
Some specialized procedures have significant waiting lists

quiz.q: Brazil's SUS is notable for being the world's largest public health system measured by what?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's SUS serves approximately 150-160 million people — roughly 75% of Brazil's population — making it the world's largest public health system by population served. It provides universal healthcare guaranteed by the 1988 Constitution, from primary care to complex surgeries.

laws.title: Constituição Federal 1988 — Redemocratization
laws.subtitle: 'Citizen Constitution' — rights after military dictatorship
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's 1988 Constitution, known as the 'Constituição Cidadã' (Citizen Constitution), established democracy after 21 years of military rule (1964-1985). It guarantees extensive social rights including health, education, housing, and food. The Constitution is among the world's longest, with 250 articles and over 100 amendments. It created the Federal Supreme Court (STF) as guardian, the Public Prosecution (Ministério Público) as independent watchdog, and federal public defenders. The Constitution is amended frequently through PECs (proposed constitutional amendments).
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations by public officials: impeachment, removal from office, criminal prosecution (crimes of responsibility).
exceptions: Constitutional amendments (PECs) can modify most provisions with 3/5 majority in two rounds
'Eternity clauses' (cláusulas pétreas) cannot be amended: federalism, separation of powers, direct vote, individual rights
States have their own constitutions within federal framework

quiz.q: What nickname was given to Brazil's 1988 Constitution?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's 1988 Constitution is nicknamed the 'Constituição Cidadã' (Citizen Constitution) because it guaranteed extensive civil rights and social rights after 21 years of military dictatorship. President Ulysses Guimarães coined the term upon the constitution's promulgation.

laws.title: Plano Real — Currency Stabilization
laws.subtitle: 1994 currency reform ended hyperinflation
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Plano Real (1994), implemented by Finance Minister Fernando Henrique Cardoso, ended hyperinflation that had reached 2,477% annually in 1993. The plan introduced the new currency (Real) pegged to the US dollar, cut government spending, and implemented monetary reforms. Inflation fell from over 2,000% to under 10% within a year. The plan's success launched Cardoso's presidency. The Real became one of Latin America's most stable currencies. Brazil's inflation management (SELIC rate target system) is now considered a model.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties — monetary policy is administrative. Currency fraud: criminal prosecution under financial crimes law.
exceptions: BRL floated against USD since 1999
Central Bank operates independently since 2021
Foreign currency transactions require Banco Central reporting above thresholds
laws.sourceLabel: Banco Central do Brasil — História do Real

quiz.q: What was Brazil's approximate annual inflation rate in 1993, before the Plano Real?
quiz.explanation: Brazil experienced annual inflation of approximately 2,477% in 1993, just before the Plano Real was implemented. The 1994 currency reform — which introduced the Real pegged to the US dollar — reduced inflation to under 10% within a year, ending decades of hyperinflationary cycles.

laws.title: Lei de Migração — Migration Law
laws.subtitle: Law 13.445/2017 — rights-based migration framework
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lei de Migração (Law 13.445/2017) replaced the 1980 Foreigners' Statute with a human rights-based approach to migration. The law guarantees migrants basic rights equal to Brazilian citizens (healthcare, education, access to justice), establishes pathways for regularization, and facilitates regional migration (especially Venezuelan refugees). Brazil has received over 400,000 Venezuelan migrants under Operation Welcome. The law reflects Brazil's 1988 Constitutional commitment to human dignity and its history as a migrant-receiving nation.
laws.penalty: Irregular entry: administrative fine, deportation. Overstay: deportation order. Human trafficking: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Mercosul citizens have preferential entry rights
Refugees under UNHCR protection have status separate from migration law
Stateless persons have specific protection procedures

quiz.q: Brazil's Lei de Migração replaced which older law?
quiz.explanation: The 2017 Lei de Migração replaced the 1980 Foreigners' Statute, which was enacted during the military dictatorship and viewed migration through a security lens. The new law takes a human rights approach, guaranteeing migrants basic rights equal to Brazilian citizens.

laws.title: Estatuto da Cidade — Urban Land Reform
laws.subtitle: Law 10.257/2001 — progressive property rights
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Estatuto da Cidade (Law 10.257/2001) established the social function of urban property. It allows municipalities to apply progressive property taxes on underused land, grants usucapião (adverse possession) after 5 years for those using abandoned urban land as primary residence, and mandates urban master plans for cities over 20,000 people. The law legalized informal settlements (favelas) by allowing regularization of land tenure. It also created participatory democracy requirements for urban planning.
laws.penalty: Underused land: progressive IPTU (property tax) up to 15% annually. Failure to comply with building requirements: compulsory purchase.
exceptions: Rural land governed by separate Estatuto da Terra
Indigenous and quilombola lands governed by constitutional provisions
Properties under federal protection have different rules

quiz.q: What does Brazil's Estatuto da Cidade allow municipalities to do with underutilized urban land?
options: Apply progressive property taxes up to 15% annually
Exempt it from all taxes to attract investment
quiz.explanation: The Estatuto da Cidade allows municipalities to apply progressive IPTU (property tax) increases of up to 15% annually on underutilized urban land. If owners still don't develop the land after the maximum tax rate, municipalities can compulsorily purchase it at tax assessment value.

laws.title: Lei de Drogas — Drug Policy
laws.subtitle: Law 11.343/2006 — decriminalization of personal use
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lei de Drogas (Law 11.343/2006) differentiates between drug trafficking and personal use. Personal possession for personal use results in non-criminal penalties: community service, educational measures, or treatment — no imprisonment. However, Brazilian courts often reclassify personal use as trafficking based on quantity and circumstances. The Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that possessing marijuana for personal use cannot be criminalized. Drug trafficking carries 5-15 years imprisonment. Brazil's drug market is dominated by the PCC and CV criminal organizations.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 5-15 years. Personal use: community service/treatment, no imprisonment. Association: 3-10 years.
exceptions: Quantity thresholds distinguishing use from trafficking are not set by law — decided by judges
Medical cannabis regulated separately by ANVISA since 2019
Ayahuasca (ceremonial use) legal since 1987 CONFEN decision

quiz.q: What is the penalty for personal drug use under Brazil's Lei de Drogas?
options: Community service or treatment — no imprisonment
Mandatory drug rehabilitation with house arrest
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Lei de Drogas decriminalized personal drug use — possession for personal use results in non-criminal penalties: community service, educational attendance, or treatment. There is no imprisonment. However, courts have discretion to classify possession as trafficking based on quantity and circumstances.

laws.title: SNUC — National System of Conservation Units
laws.subtitle: Law 9.985/2000 — biodiversity protection framework
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's SNUC (Sistema Nacional de Unidades de Conservação, Law 9.985/2000) established a national system of protected areas covering over 150 million hectares — about 18% of Brazil's territory. Protected areas include strict nature reserves (integral protection) and sustainable use areas (where traditional communities may live). IBAMA and ICMBio manage federal protected areas. Brazil has the world's most diverse fauna and flora. Deforestation in the Amazon creates pressure on protected areas and indigenous territories.
laws.penalty: Activities prohibited in conservation units: fines, criminal prosecution (1-5 years). Damage to fauna: 6 months-1 year.
exceptions: Sustainable use units (APA, RESEX) allow traditional and commercial activities under management plans
Indigenous lands within conservation units governed by FUNAI and FUNAI/ICMBio agreements
Research with permits allowed in all categories

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Brazil's territory is covered by SNUC protected areas?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's SNUC system protects approximately 150 million hectares — about 18% of national territory. Combined with indigenous lands (another 13%), roughly one-third of Brazil has some form of territorial protection, though enforcement remains a major challenge.

laws.title: Lei Rouanet — Cultural Incentive Law
laws.subtitle: Law 8.313/1991 — tax incentives for cultural funding
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Lei Rouanet (Law 8.313/1991) allows companies and individuals to direct a portion of their income tax to approved cultural projects. Companies can redirect up to 4% of income tax, individuals up to 6%. The Secretaria Especial da Cultura approves projects and manages the PRONAC (National Arts and Culture Support Program). The law has funded cinema, theater, music, and museums. Critics argue large companies dominate project selection for marketing purposes. The law is credited with reviving Brazil's film industry.
laws.penalty: Fraud in Lei Rouanet applications: criminal prosecution, repayment with interest, disqualification.
exceptions: Small cultural projects below threshold use simplified Mecenato Simplificado
Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian cultural projects have priority status
Educational institutions have separate cultural funding frameworks

quiz.q: Under Brazil's Lei Rouanet, what maximum percentage of income tax can companies redirect to cultural projects?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Lei Rouanet allows companies to redirect up to 4% of their income tax to approved cultural projects, and individuals up to 6%. The law has been instrumental in funding Brazilian cinema, theater, and music, though it has been criticized for allowing sponsors to control project selection for marketing benefit.

laws.title: Simples Nacional — Simplified Business Tax
laws.subtitle: Complementary Law 123/2006 — unified SME taxation
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Simples Nacional (Complementary Law 123/2006) created a unified tax regime for micro and small businesses, replacing multiple federal, state, and municipal taxes with a single monthly payment. Businesses with annual revenues up to R$4.8 million qualify. Tax rates range from 4-19% depending on revenue bracket and sector. Simples Nacional simplified Brazil's notoriously complex tax system for small businesses and is credited with formalizing millions of businesses. Individual micro-entrepreneurs (MEI) have a simplified version with flat monthly payments.
laws.penalty: Disqualification from Simples Nacional for tax debts: return to regular tax regime. Tax fraud: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: MEI (Individual Micro-Entrepreneur) has separate simplified regime
Financial institutions and some regulated sectors excluded
Companies with equity participation in other companies excluded

quiz.q: What is the maximum annual revenue for a business to qualify for Brazil's Simples Nacional tax regime?
quiz.explanation: Brazil's Simples Nacional covers businesses with annual revenues up to R$4.8 million (empresas de pequeno porte). Micro enterprises (microempresas) qualify up to R$360,000. Individual micro-entrepreneurs (MEI) have an even simpler regime up to R$81,000 annually.

laws.title: Reforma Trabalhista — Labor Reform
laws.subtitle: Law 13.467/2017 — modernization of CLT
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's Labor Reform (Law 13.467/2017) significantly modified the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT, 1943). Key changes: intermittent (zero-hours) contracts legalized, collective bargaining agreements can override CLT on some issues, outsourcing of core activities permitted, home-office regulated, and union contributions made voluntary (ending mandatory union tax). The reform was controversial — unions argued it weakened protections, while business argued it reduced informal employment. Union membership and revenues fell significantly post-reform.
laws.penalty: Employer CLT violations: labor court fines, back pay with FGTS deposits, severance payments.
exceptions: Workers earning over twice the INSS ceiling have modified negotiation rights
Domestic workers (empregadas domésticas) have separate Constitutional rights
Rural workers have some distinct CLT provisions

quiz.q: What did Brazil's 2017 Labor Reform do to union contribution fees?
options: Doubled them to fund worker retraining
Made them voluntary (ended mandatory union tax)
Transferred them to the federal government
quiz.explanation: Brazil's 2017 Labor Reform made union dues voluntary, ending the mandatory 'contribuição sindical' — a union tax equivalent to one day's salary per year that all workers paid regardless of union membership. This significantly reduced union revenues and membership.

laws.title: Demarcação de Terras Indígenas
laws.subtitle: Indigenous land demarcation — constitutional right
laws.fullDescription: Brazil's 1988 Constitution (Article 231) recognized indigenous peoples' rights to their traditional territories and established a process for official demarcation. FUNAI (National Indian Foundation) conducts demarcation studies. Demarcated indigenous lands cover about 13% of Brazil's territory, mostly in the Amazon. The Supreme Court's Marco Temporal ruling (2023) — and its subsequent partial reversal by Congress — caused major controversy. Indigenous communities clashed with agribusiness interests over land rights. Uninvited entry into demarcated indigenous land is a federal crime.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized occupation of indigenous land: federal crime, removal, civil damages. Violence against indigenous people: federal jurisdiction.
exceptions: Mining in indigenous lands requires congressional authorization (rarely granted)
Existing settlements within demarcated areas have transition provisions
Federal infrastructure projects require indigenous consultation (though often insufficient)
laws.sourceLabel: FUNAI — Fundação Nacional dos Povos Indígenas

quiz.q: What percentage of Brazil's territory is covered by officially demarcated indigenous lands?
quiz.explanation: Officially demarcated indigenous lands cover approximately 13% of Brazil's national territory, mostly in the Amazon region. Brazil's 1988 Constitution recognized indigenous peoples' rights to their traditional territories, and FUNAI manages the demarcation and protection of these areas.
